title: Meet the Karigars: Jaipur Block Printing, Step by Step From Sanganer
excerpt: Meet the karigars behind Jaipur block printing: the Sanganer and Bagru craft, from carving wooden blocks to the final wash, explained step by step.
body:
Jaipur block printing is a hand craft in which karigars stamp patterns onto fabric using carved wooden blocks, one impression at a time. It has been practised in and around Jaipur for centuries, especially in the printing towns of Sanganer and Bagru, and every hand block printed kurta still passes through the same patient steps. Here is how the craft works, and why each piece is a little different.

## A short history of Rajasthan block printing

Block printing in India is very old, and Rajasthan became one of its great centres. Under royal patronage in the Jaipur region, printing communities, known traditionally as chhipas, settled near water sources where they could wash and dye cloth. Two towns near Jaipur became famous for very different styles.

| Centre | Typical style | Look and feel |
|---|---|---|
| Sanganer | Fine floral and paisley motifs, delicate outlines | Light or white grounds, soft and airy |
| Bagru | Bold, earthy motifs, often with dabu mud resist | Deeper grounds, natural dye tones |

Sanganer prints are known for small buttis, trailing flowers and fine detail, while Bagru is associated with dabu, a resist method using a paste of mud, gum and other natural materials. Both traditions are still alive today, and the motifs you see on modern kurtas, from anar (pomegranate) to tiny florals, often come straight from these old pattern books.

## The process, step by step

### Step 1: Designing and carving the block

Every print begins as a drawing. The design is transferred onto a smooth block of hardwood, usually sheesham or teak, and a skilled block carver chisels away the background by hand so the pattern stands in relief.

A single design usually needs several blocks: one for the outline, called the rekh, and separate blocks for each colour that fills it, often called gadh or datta. Carving is slow, precise work, and a well-made block can be used for many years.

### Step 2: Preparing the fabric

Before printing, the cotton is washed to remove starch and impurities so the colour can soak in evenly. In traditional methods it may be treated with harda (myrobalan), which gives a pale yellow base and helps certain natural dyes fix to the cloth. The fabric is then dried in the sun and smoothed out.

### Step 3: Printing by hand

This is the heart of the craft. The fabric is pinned flat on a long padded table. The printer dips the block into a tray of colour, positions it carefully, and presses it down with a firm strike of the palm. Then they lift it, move it along, and repeat, matching each impression to the last by eye.

The outline block goes first. Once it dries, the colour blocks follow, each placed exactly inside the outline. This is why hand block prints have their gentle charm: tiny variations in pressure and alignment that a machine never makes. The [Coral Pink Hand Block Print Cotton Tunic Top](/products/coral-pink-hand-block-print-cotton-tunic-top/) shows this softness in its anar motif.

### Step 4: Dyeing, drying and fixing

After printing, the fabric is dried, often in long rows in the sun. Depending on the method, it may be dyed in a vat, steamed or treated so the colours set. For dabu prints, the fabric is dyed after the mud paste is applied, and the paste is washed away to reveal the resisted pattern beneath.

The cloth is then washed thoroughly to remove excess colour and any remaining paste. This is the moment when the print truly comes alive.

## From printed fabric to finished kurta

Finally, the fabric is dried, ironed and checked. Only then is it cut and stitched into a kurta, tunic or dress. ## How to recognise and care for a real block print

- **Look for tiny irregularities.** Slight overlaps or gaps where blocks meet are a sign of hand work, not a defect.
- **Check the back.** Hand printed colour often shows faintly through the reverse side.
- **Wash gently.** Use cold water, mild detergent and dry in the shade so the colours stay bright.
- **Wash separately at first.** Some colour release is normal in the first few washes.

## Frequently asked questions

**What is the difference between Sanganer and Bagru prints?**
Sanganer prints usually have fine floral motifs on light grounds, while Bagru prints are bolder and often use dabu mud resist with deeper, earthy colours.

**Why are no two block printed kurtas exactly the same?**
Each impression is placed and pressed by hand, so small variations in alignment and colour are natural and part of the beauty.

**Does hand block print fade?**
Some softening over time is normal. Cold hand washing and drying in the shade keep the colours looking fresh for longer.

**What wood are printing blocks made from?**
Traditionally hardwoods such as sheesham or teak, which are strong enough to be carved finely and used for years.
